64.title: Remember me (Luke 23:32–43)
64.hook: a dying thief asks to be remembered and is promised paradise today
64.howItsDone: Catholics hear the good thief's words in the Passion on Good Friday, and many ask Saint Dismas to pray for the dying and for people in prison.

segments.voice: Yesterday, before Pilate: are you a king, and the washed hands. Your line was what is truth. A new week: the cross and the morning.

A hill outside the city walls, called the place of the skull. Calvary, in the old Latin. Three crosses: Jesus in the middle, a criminal on each side. The crowd watches. Soldiers cast lots for his clothes. And the first thing Luke has Jesus say from the cross, in the Douay-Rheims, is this: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." Then the men beside him start talking. One joins the mocking: if you're the Christ, save yourself, and us. And the other, who has nothing left, no time, no chance to make anything right, turns his head and says something nobody expects.
screen: `THE PLACE OF THE SKULL.` → `FATHER, FORGIVE THEM.` → `TWO MEN, TWO VERY DIFFERENT WORDS.`

segments.voice: He tells the first man to stop. We deserve this, he says, but this man has done nothing wrong. Then, to Jesus: "Lord, remember me when thou shalt come into thy kingdom." No speech. No list of what he did. Notice what he calls the man dying next to him: Lord. And what he asks for: not to be taken down from the cross, only to be remembered. Jesus answers: "Amen I say to thee, this day thou shalt be with me in paradise." Paradise is a Persian word that came into Greek. It first meant a walled garden, the kind a king kept. Jewish writers used it for the garden of Eden, and then for the place where God keeps the righteous. So a man dying on a cross is promised a garden, and not someday. This day. Luke never gives his name. Later Christian writings call him Dismas, and Catholics know him as the good thief, honored as a saint; some ask his prayers for the dying and for prisoners. Look at what the text leaves out. No baptism is mentioned. No time to make amends, no list of sins, no promise to do better. One honest sentence, at the very end. The Church reads this story as a sign that mercy can reach anyone, right up to the last breath.

segments.voice: No long list, no explaining yourself: just notice what it's like to want to be remembered, by someone you love, or by God, and let the wanting be there without dressing it up. If you pray, you can use the thief's own words, slowly, a few times: Lord, remember me. If you don't, you can just hold the wish quietly and breathe.

65.title: His mother stood (John 19:25–27)
65.hook: Mary at the foot of the cross, given to the beloved disciple as his mother
65.howItsDone: Catholics sing or pray the Stabat Mater during the Stations of the Cross, especially in Lent, and honor Mary as Mother of the Church on the Monday after Pentecost.

segments.voice: Yesterday, remember me: a dying thief asked for one thing and was promised a garden. Your line was this day in paradise. Now, the ones who stayed.

A hospital corridor at three in the morning. Nothing to do. Nothing to fix. People stay because leaving is unthinkable. Now, the hill. Mark says that at the arrest his disciples all left him and fled. But John's Gospel slows down and names who is standing by the cross: his mother, and his mother's sister, Mary of Cleophas, and Mary Magdalen. And one disciple, never named, whom the Gospel calls the disciple whom Jesus loved. They can't stop it. They can't change any of it. They stand.
screen: `NOTHING TO FIX. THEY STAY.` → `THE WOMEN AND ONE DISCIPLE.` → `THEY STAND.`

segments.voice: Jesus spends some of his last words on this. In the Douay-Rheims: "Woman, behold thy son." And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother." John adds: "And from that hour, the disciple took her to his own." Woman can sound cold in English. In John it's the same word he used for her at the wedding at Cana, a word of respect, and some readers hear an echo of the first woman in Genesis. Catholics hear this moment two ways, and hold both. The first is simple and human: a dying son makes sure his mother will have a home. The second is bigger. The Gospel never names the beloved disciple. Tradition says it was John. Some readers say leaving him unnamed lets every disciple stand in his place. So Catholics read it as Jesus giving his mother to all of us, and they call Mary the Mother of the Church, a title Pope Paul VI gave her during the Second Vatican Council. Then there's the word stood. In the Latin Bible the verse opens with stabant, they stood, all of them together. A medieval hymn takes the word for her alone: Stabat Mater, the mother stood. It belongs to the feast of Our Lady of Sorrows, and parishes sing it at the Stations of the Cross. She didn't faint. She didn't leave. She stood.

66.title: It is finished (Luke 23:44–56)
66.hook: darkness, the veil torn, into thy hands, and a borrowed tomb
66.howItsDone: On Good Friday Catholics celebrate no Mass; they gather for the Passion, prayers, the veneration of the cross and communion from hosts consecrated the night before, and the Church's night prayer repeats the words into your hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Stabat Mater: his mother stood at the foot of the cross, and he gave her to his friend. Your line was behold thy mother. Today is the hardest hour of the story.

A Catholic church on Good Friday afternoon looks wrong on purpose. The tabernacle stands open and empty. The altar is stripped bare: no cloth, no candles, no flowers. There's no Mass; on this day and the next, the Church celebrates none. The priest walks in and lies face down on the floor, or kneels, in silence. Then the Passion is read aloud, the whole story, and at one moment everyone in the church kneels, and nobody says a word for a while. Today is that moment, the way Luke tells it.

It's about noon, and Luke says darkness covers the whole land until three. In the Douay-Rheims: "And the sun was darkened, and the veil of the temple was rent in the midst." The veil was the great curtain in the temple that hid the holiest place, where only the high priest went, once a year. Christians have read its tearing as the way to God being opened. Then Jesus cries out with a loud voice: "Father, into thy hands I commend my spirit." Those words aren't new. They're from a psalm of trust, Psalm thirty in the Douay-Rheims, and he dies praying it. Today's title comes from John's Gospel, where the Douay-Rheims renders it "It is consummated." In Greek it's one word, tetelestai: it is finished, brought to its end. Two Gospels, two last words, and the Church keeps both. Then small, human things. A Roman centurion who has watched it all says: "Indeed this was a just man." The crowds go home beating their breasts. A council member named Joseph, from a town called Arimathea, who had not agreed with the others, asks Pilate for the body, wraps it in linen, and lays it in a tomb cut from rock where no one had ever been laid. The women from Galilee follow to see where. They go home, prepare spices, and rest on the Sabbath, as the law asked. And the Church's night prayer, at the end of every day, takes up his last words again: into your hands.

67.title: Holy Saturday
67.hook: the day of silence; the Church says he went down to free the dead (CCC 632–635)
67.carry: god is in the silence too
67.howItsDone: On Holy Saturday Catholic churches celebrate no Mass during the day; the tabernacle stays empty, and the Church waits in prayer until the Easter Vigil after nightfall.

segments.voice: Yesterday, tetelestai, it is finished: darkness, the veil torn, a psalm on his lips, and a tomb cut from rock. Your line was into thy hands. Today, the day after.

Everyone knows a day in between. The day after the phone call and before the funeral. The day you wait for a test result. Nothing happens, and it's the heaviest day of the week. The Gospels say almost nothing about the Saturday after the cross. Matthew mentions guards posted at the tomb. Luke gives it one line: the women rested on the Sabbath, according to the commandment. No words from Jesus. No miracles. A sealed tomb, and people sitting at home with spices they can't use yet. The Church keeps that day on purpose: on Holy Saturday there's no Mass during the day, and the tabernacle is still empty. Catholics wait.
screen: `THE DAY IN BETWEEN.` → `ALMOST NOTHING IN THE GOSPELS.` → `THE CHURCH WAITS.`

segments.voice: But the Church doesn't say nothing happened. It says something happened where no one could see. In the old Apostles' Creed, Catholics say: "He descended into hell." That word trips people up. Here it doesn't mean the place of the damned. The Catechism explains it means the realm of all the dead, what the Hebrew Bible calls Sheol. Jesus really died, the Church says, so he went where the dead go. Not to be stuck there: to open it, to bring out the just who had died before him, all the way back to Adam and Eve. The First Letter of Peter says he went and preached to the spirits in prison. Eastern Christians paint it. Their Easter icon doesn't show an empty tomb. It shows Christ standing on broken doors, the locks scattered, pulling Adam and Eve up out of their graves by the wrists. And an ancient sermon read on Holy Saturday in the Church's daily prayer, the Office of Readings, begins by saying there is a great silence on the earth, because the King is asleep. Then it follows him down, looking for Adam. So on the quietest day of the year, the Church says God was at work in the deepest place. Nobody saw it. It didn't make a sound. Silence isn't the same as absence.

Hold it the way the women held their spices, ready and not yet used; you don't have to understand it or fix it. If you pray, you can simply stay in God's presence without words; if you don't, you can notice what silence actually sounds like.

68.title: Mary Magdalene in the garden (John 20:1–18)
68.hook: she thinks he's the gardener until he says her name
68.howItsDone: Catholics hear John's account of Mary Magdalene at the tomb on Easter Sunday morning, and keep her feast on 22 July as the apostle to the apostles.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Holy Saturday, the silent day, when the Church says he went down to free the dead. Your line was god is in the silence too. Now, it's morning.

A name is a strange thing. A stranger reads it off a list and it's just a word. Someone who knows you says it once, quietly, across a crowded room, and it lands differently. Early on the first day of the week, while it's still dark, Mary Magdalene walks to the tomb. The stone has been rolled away. The body is gone. She runs for Peter; they come, look, and go home. She stays outside the tomb, crying.
screen: `A NAME, SAID BY SOMEONE WHO KNOWS YOU.` → `STILL DARK. THE STONE MOVED.` → `SHE STAYS, CRYING.`

segments.voice: She bends to look in and sees two angels, who ask why she's weeping. They've taken my Lord away, she says, and I don't know where they've laid him. She turns, and a man is standing there. In the Douay-Rheims he asks: "Woman, why weepest thou? whom seekest thou?" She thinks he's the gardener. Sir, she says, if you've moved him, tell me where, and I'll take him. Then he says one word. "Mary." Not a proof. Not a speech. Her name. And she turns and says: "Rabboni," which John explains means Master, my teacher. Notice the Gospel's honesty: she doesn't recognize the risen Jesus by his face. She knows him by the way he says her name. Then he sends her: go to my brothers, and tell them. She goes to the disciples and says: "I have seen the Lord." In John's Gospel she is the first to see him risen, sent to tell the ones who will tell everyone else. The Church calls her the apostle to the apostles, and in 2016 Pope Francis raised her day, 22 July, to a feast, like the apostles' own. One more thing to clear up. Later preaching called her a repentant prostitute. The Gospels never say that. It came from sermons, Pope Gregory the Great's among them, that blended her with other women in the Gospels, and the Church's calendar separated them again in 1969.

69.title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
69.hook: two sad friends walk seven miles with a stranger and know him in the breaking of bread
69.howItsDone: Catholics hear the Emmaus story in the Easter season, and the Catechism sees in it the two parts of every Mass: the Liturgy of the Word and the Liturgy of the Eucharist.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene in the garden: she took him for the gardener until he said her name, and she answered, Rabboni. Your line was he says your name. Now, the walk home.

Same Sunday, late afternoon. Two of Jesus's followers are walking home from Jerusalem to a village called Emmaus, sixty furlongs away, Luke says, about seven miles. One is named Cleophas. The other, Luke never names. They go over it again and again, the way people do on the long drive home from a funeral. A stranger falls into step beside them and asks what they're talking about. They stop. Their faces fall. Are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who hasn't heard? Then the words that give it all away: we had hoped he was the one. Had hoped. Past tense.
screen: `SEVEN MILES, WALKING HOME.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.` → `WE HAD HOPED.`

segments.voice: The stranger is Jesus, but Luke says their eyes were held so they didn't know him. He doesn't reveal himself. He walks with them and opens the Scriptures, from Moses through all the prophets, showing how the Messiah had to suffer and so enter his glory. Seven miles of Bible study. At the village he acts as if he's going further, and they beg him, in the Douay-Rheims: "Stay with us, because it is towards evening, and the day is now far spent." He goes in. At the table he takes the bread, blesses it, breaks it and gives it to them: the same four movements as the Last Supper. Their eyes are opened, they know him, and he vanishes. They turn to each other: "Was not our heart burning within us, whilst he spoke in the way, and opened to us the scriptures?" That same hour, Luke says, they walk the seven miles back, to tell the others how they knew him "in the breaking of bread." The Catechism sees the shape of the Mass in this road. First the Word: the Scriptures read and opened. Then the table: bread taken, blessed, broken, given. Two parts, in the order Luke tells it. And notice where he's recognized. Not in the explaining, as good as it was. In the bread. Pope John Paul II named a letter on the Eucharist after their plea: stay with us, Lord.

70.title: Thomas (John 20:24–29)
70.hook: he wanted to touch the wounds, and then said my Lord and my God
70.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of Thomas every year on the Second Sunday of Easter, and some quietly say 'my Lord and my God' when the host is raised at Mass.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road to Emmaus: seven miles with a stranger, and bread broken at the end. Your line was was not our heart burning. Today, the one who wasn't there.

There's a phrase for people like Thomas: pics or it didn't happen. On Easter night the risen Jesus comes to the disciples behind shut doors, and Thomas isn't there. When the others tell him, we have seen the Lord, he doesn't believe a word. In the Douay-Rheims he says: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the place of the nails, and put my hand into his side, I will not believe." Not just see. Touch. People still call him doubting Thomas.
screen: `PICS OR IT DIDN'T HAPPEN.` → `THOMAS WASN'T THERE.` → `I WILL NOT BELIEVE.`

segments.voice: First, who Thomas was. Earlier in John, when Jesus decides to go back into Judea, where people had just tried to stone him, it's Thomas who says: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." Not a coward. Blunt, loyal, and he won't pretend. Eight days after Easter they're together again, the doors shut, and this time Thomas is there. Jesus stands in the middle and says, "Peace be to you." Then he offers Thomas exactly what he asked for: put in your finger, see my hands, bring your hand, put it into my side, "and be not faithless, but believing." He doesn't scold him for asking. He shows him the wounds. And here's the surprise: the Gospel never says Thomas touched them. What it gives us is his answer: "My Lord, and my God." The man remembered for doubting is the one who says it. Then Jesus adds a line for everyone after: "blessed are they that have not seen, and have believed." Christians hear themselves in that line. Catholics hear this Gospel every year on the Sunday after Easter, and by an old custom, when the priest lifts the host at Mass, some people whisper Thomas's words: my Lord and my God. Tradition says Thomas later carried the faith all the way to India, and Christians there still call themselves Saint Thomas Christians. So that was the week: remember me, the Stabat Mater, tetelestai, Holy Saturday, the garden, Emmaus, and Thomas.
screen: `LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE WITH HIM.` · `HE SHOWS HIM THE WOUNDS.` · `NO VERSE SAYS HE TOUCHED THEM.` · `THE DOUBTER'S CONFESSION.` · then, large: `MY LORD, AND MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Name one thing about faith, or God, or your own life, that you're not sure about; don't hide it and don't force an answer, just hold it in the open, the way Thomas said his out loud to his friends. If you pray, you can bring it to God as plainly as he did; in the story, Jesus didn't turn him away.
Thomas. The disciple who wanted to see and touch, and who then said: my Lord and my God. Today's word.
Your line: doubt can kneel too. Honest questions have a place. Seventy days, ten weeks.
